    Tech Report: AI Native Right Hand of the CEO - EdTech (French fluent 🇫🇷) at Paradox

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You dream of a new challenge, of being able to make a company scale and feel that you have a real impact.
    • If you dream of a life that is more like an adventure than a stable life, then becoming the AI-native right hand of our CEO is for you.
    • This isn’t another chief of staff or right hand job.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You dream of a new challenge, of being able to make a company scale and feel that you have a real impact.

    If you dream of a life that is more like an adventure than a stable life, then becoming the AI-native right hand of our CEO is for you.

    This isn’t another chief of staff or right hand job.

    It has been revealed that most companies call themselves AI-first because they gave everyone a ChatGPT licence. We think that’s level 2, and there are 10.

    According to recent reports, at Paradox our ambition is $10M in revenue with 10 people, each of them running a dozen agents. Here, AI doesn’t assist the work. It runs the loops, in every department. Your job is to make that true for the whole tech giant, side by side with the CEO.

    Deep inside you are looking for a new adventure with….

    🗽Freedom: working remotely or hybrid, and being trusted to deliver.

    🔥Ambition: building one of the first truly AI-native companies, with teammates who push AI to its limits every week.

    😍Impact: changing the trajectory of a whole firm, not one line of a roadmap, with a product that transforms people’s lives at scale.

    Then, you have found the next adventure that will fulfill you.

    Recent findings suggest that in a company of fewer than 10 people, the right hand used to be the person who absorbed everything the CEO couldn’t do. Here, the right hand builds the machine that does it.

    In a recent development, hold the full context of Paradox. Our DNA, offers, decisions, procedures, member stories and past experiments, in one shared manufacturer brain that every person and every agent reads before acting.

    Sources indicate that turn every decision into execution. A meeting, a voice note or a call with the CEO becomes briefs, tickets, follow-ups and deadlines, without anyone retyping it.

    In a recent development, act across every tool. Not a chatbot in a tab: agents read and write in our whole stack, from code to CRM, billing, analytics, ads, email, calendar and documents.

    Ship. Produce the analysis, the contract draft, the page, the offer or the process, and put it live.

    Measure with real KPIs. Revenue, cash, margin, retention and the transformation of our members, not activity.

    Industry observers note that learn and loop on its own. Keep what works, kill what doesn’t, write the lesson back into the brain, and start the next cycle without waiting for a meeting.

    People set the ambition, the taste and the standards. The machine runs the loop, and gets better every week.

    According to recent reports, this is already real. Our company brain holds our decisions and procedures. Our growth hub tracks every hypothesis and experiment with its result. Agents cut ads from long-form content, prepare webinars and audit our tracking after every live. And our product is AI-native too: Athena, our AI coach, works with members every day, by text and by voice.

    Sources indicate that we believe self-help is broken. Most people use learning platforms the same way: generic theory, a quick high, no real change.

    They deserve more than content and more than motivation.

    They deserve a system that knows them, one that adapts, challenges and grows with them.

    Human Intelligence (coaches, peers and mentors).

    Structured Intelligence (protocols, mental models, rituals).

    Technological Intelligence (AI personalization, feedback loops, adaptive journeys).

    into one seamless ecosystem: Paradox OS, the Operating System for Human Greatness, augmented with AI.

    Industry observers note that paradox was founded by David Laroche, a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson and Gad Elmaleh. We started in French. We’re building for the world, and for something that will outlive any individual, its founder included.

    Here’s the bet: A small team running a self-learning machine can out-test, out-learn and out-grow teams a hundred times its size.

    Reporting directly to the founder and CEO, you will help him run and grow the company.

    Your scope is as wide as a CEO/COO’s: strategy, operations, finance, legal, people, product marketing and launches.

    The difference is how you do it. In a classic company, the right hand coordinates people and AI helps. Here it’s the other way round: agents do the work, you design the system, set the bar and make the calls. With fewer than 10 people, there is no department to hand things to. You build it.

    ❌The old way: a chief of staff takes notes in meetings, chases people by email and builds the weekly report by hand.

    According to recent reports, 🏴‍☠️At Paradox: you build the agents that turn every CEO decision into execution. Meetings, voice notes and calls become briefs, tickets and follow-ups. Every Monday, the CEO gets one brief: what moved, what’s stuck, and what needs his call.

    It has been revealed that you decide what the CEO must see and what he never needs to see again. His time goes to vision, product and members, not to coordination.

    Depending on your zone of genius, these are examples of strategic projects you could own:.

    Growth: run experiments with agents that generate, ship and measure them.

    Partnerships & sponsorships: find and close partners aligned with our brand, for our YouTube channel and events.

    International: build the machine that turns our French content into English, and open latest countries.

    Launches: take a newly introduced offer or product from idea to live.

    People: find and assess the rare people who join a team of fewer than 10.

    ❌The old way: each fresh initiative needs a team, a roadmap and three months.

    Recent findings suggest that 🏴‍☠️At Paradox: one person with the right agents rolls out an offer, a channel or a country without disrupting the core. That’s what our Pirate Squad means now.

    ❌The old way: an ops manager processes invoices, chases contracts, onboards people and answers the same support questions every week.

    🏴‍☠️At Paradox: finance, legal, HR, admin and customer support each get their agents, their context, their KPIs and their loop. You write the skills, plug them into our tools and write the evals that define "good": a reconciliation that matches to the cent, a contract that respects our playbook, an answer a member is happy with.

    You give autonomy step by step: first an agent suggests, then it acts once you approve, then it acts alone within a budget and guardrails. An agent moves up a level only when its track record earns it.

    Example: in your first month, you build the agent that reconciles payments, refunds and failed charges every night. In month one it only reports. By month three it fixes the simple cases alone, and you only see the exceptions.

    ❌The old way: someone builds dashboards in a BI tool, exports them to a spreadsheet at the end of the month, and nobody fully trusts the numbers.

    🏴‍☠️At Paradox: agents watch revenue, cash, acquisition, retention, churn and competitors continuously, find where our sources disagree, and explain what changed and why.

    Strategy: screen markets and competition, build growth models, explore business models, partnerships and acquisitions. Then challenge, formalize and ensure good execution of the strategy.

    At Paradox things move fast, and our CEO is always reading business books and meeting great entrepreneurs. You’ll turn the best strategies and tactics into systems and agents the whole manufacturer uses.

    ❌The old way: lessons live in people’s heads and leave with them.

    🏴‍☠️At Paradox: every decision, result and lesson goes back into the company brain, and agents read it before acting. The company never learns the same lesson twice.

    You measure the machine itself: the share of work done without a human, the time from decision to execution, the agents that moved up an autonomy level this month, and revenue per person. You push those numbers up.

    You help the team become AI-native too: you spot the work still done by hand, and you build the agent or show a teammate how to build it.

    It has been revealed that and always: our members trust us with their lives. No fake claims, no fake scarcity, data handled with care. The machine can scale, but it doesn’t decide what’s right. People do.

    Recent findings suggest that how you’ll know you’re AI-native: you spend your time building agents, writing evals and making calls, not doing the work by hand. The organization’s output grows every month while the headcount doesn’t.

    Top tier Business or Engineering School (HEC, ESSEC, INSEAD, EM Lyon, EDHEC, ESCP, Stanford, …) or other high-level academic training (Les Mines, X, Sciences Po Paris, etc.).

    A wide-scope role behind you: founder, chief of staff, founder’s associate, strategy, consulting or operations in a fast-growing startup.

    Industry observers note that you’ve built with AI and agents yourself: Claude Code, agent SDKs, MCP, automations, APIs, evals. Show us something you built, not a certificate.

    Driven with strong work ethic: this position requires a strong commitment and perseverance.

    Entrepreneurship spirit: able to own a project from scratch, with few resources and little guidance, doing a lot yourself.

    Builder, not coordinator: you’d rather build the agent than chase a person twice.

    Taste: you know the difference between an output that works and one that is great, and you hold agents to the second.

    Growth over ego: you are at ease with regular feedback, obsessed with learning and growing, able to put your ego aside.

    Analytical and system thinker: you promptly identify and formulate problems, and solve complex ones with data.

    Excels in communication: both written and verbal.

    According to recent reports, french: native or bilingual. English: fluent, you can hold a detailed conversation with English-speaking colleagues. Our chosen language for written communication is English.

    We are inspired by a culture of performance and ambition. Everything is fast-paced and there is a lot of change. You won’t always be told what to do or how to do it.

    According to recent reports, we tell each other things, even if they are uncomfortable. We value growth over ego. At Paradox, expressing disagreement to a manager and knowing how to debate is valued! We encourage critical and strategic thinking.

    ❌ If you use AI for first drafts but your way of working looks the same as two years ago: wrong role.

    ❌ If you want to manage a lot of people: we aim for $10M in revenue with 10 people, each managing a dozen agents.

    ❌ If you need clarity before chaos: wrong place.

    If all this makes sense with you, then we’ll love working with you (and you with us, you’ll be pampered!).

    Build one of the first truly AI-native companies from inside the CEO’s office, and write the playbook others will copy. You’ll compete with San Francisco companies.

    A work with Impact, Freedom and Ambition.

    🏅Being surrounded by A-players who strive to perform, whilst being in a good mood.

    🏋️‍♀️No more bosses, but ongoing conversations to support your growth.

    ⚡️Learning to build with AI faster than almost anywhere else.

    🦄Playing a crucial role in the development of a company whose content and products are used by millions of people.

    🤩Waking up in the morning feeling like you are making a difference is something! We receive messages every day from members who quit smoking, reached a milestone in their business, built better relationships and changed their lives.

    But that’s not all, we believe that driven people deserve….

    😎A firm culture based on autonomy & accountability.

    🗽Flexible working hours (but very hard working).

    🌎A remote culture from day one with the freedom to work from wherever you want.

    🧍‍♀️Standing desks paid by the organization if you live far from our offices.

    🏀350€ per year paid by the manufacturer to take care of yourself (for your gym, a dance class or whatever makes you feel great).

    📚150€ of books or education: at Paradox, we are learner lovers.

    🔥Access to Athena, our AI coach, supporting you on anything personal or professional.

    ❌ Any copy-pasted and non-personalized application goes directly to the trash can.

    ⚠️ To complete the recruitment process, each candidate must organize calls with his or her previous managers. If you are not comfortable with this: do not apply ⚠️.

    📃 A 6 to 8 minute application survey, with a short video and a link to something you built with AI.

    💻 A 30-minute video call with Timy, HR, to deep dive into your career path and ambitions.

    🛠️ A live build session: you solve a real Paradox problem with AI in front of us. We look at how you prompt, push back on the output and iterate, more than at a polished result.

    💻 A 1h culture-fit video call, to assess alignment with our values and mindset.

    💻 A 1h final video call with David, CEO, on the organization’s next milestones and how you’d build them.

    💼 Reference calls with your previous managers.

    If all this sounds good to you, come and write the next chapter with us 🚀🚀.

    Tech Report: Software Engineer - Interfaces Backend at Supabase

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • In a recent development, we’re looking for a Software Engineer to join Supabase’s Interfaces group and help run the backend services behind our developer tools, starting with postgres-meta: the open-source service that runs SQL against customers’ Postgres databases on behalf of our dashboard, our MCP server, AI agents, and other platform tools.
    • According to recent reports, AI agents are the fastest-growing source of postgres-meta’s traffic, and it sits on the path between developers and their data, so when it struggles, people can’t reach their databases from the dashboard or their agents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    In a recent development, we’re looking for a Software Engineer to join Supabase’s Interfaces group and help run the backend services behind our developer tools, starting with postgres-meta: the open-source service that runs SQL against customers’ Postgres databases on behalf of our dashboard, our MCP server, AI agents, and other platform tools. You’ll work closely with the engineers who build those tools, and with our Platform and SRE teams.

    According to recent reports, AI agents are the fastest-growing source of postgres-meta’s traffic, and it sits on the path between developers and their data, so when it struggles, people can’t reach their databases from the dashboard or their agents. The team’s first priority is making it reliable, observable, and fair between tenants at agent scale, and helping redesign it for that scale without breaking the tools that depend on it. Depending on your experience, you’ll own major parts of that work or lead it. Alongside it, the team builds the backend services that give every branch of a project the configuration and secrets it needs.

    Sources indicate that we want to be upfront: this role carries real operational load. Our on-call process and rotation are new and need a lot of maturing, and you’ll help build them into something sustainable from your first weeks. You’ll be on call for services on the critical path, and incidents come before planned work. Platform teams run the infrastructure underneath; you’ll own the services themselves, from their code to how they behave in production. It’s ideal for someone who enjoys that kind of ownership, thrives in async, fast-paced environments, and stays calm when the root cause turns out to be in someone else’s system.

    According to recent reports, help mature the team’s on-call from your first weeks: grow the rotation to cover every service the team runs, write runbooks, and agree when to declare an incident. Then build it, with our embedded SRE, into a sustainable follow-the-sun rotation as the team grows.

    Set SLOs with the teams that call the service, and build the observability to hold them: metrics per tenant and per caller, alerts that catch failures wherever they start, and logs you can search across regions.

    Make deploys routine with canary and staged rollouts, so dependency and security upgrades stop being risky.

    Redesign how the service works with Postgres at scale: reusing connections, limiting or streaming large results, and isolating and rate-limiting tenants, so no single caller, human or agent, can degrade it for everyone else.

    Help decide the service’s long-term architecture with our Platform teams, then evolve it without breaking the callers that depend on it.

    Write down and agree the service’s contract with its callers, including the dashboard, MCP and AI, and platform workers: how transactions, multi-statement queries, timeouts, and errors behave.

    Work through incidents with the networking, Kubernetes, pooler, and control-plane teams when a problem on the path to customers’ databases starts in their systems.

    Build backend services for code-first workflows, starting with delivering each branch’s configuration and secrets to the services that need them.

    Make small changes directly in the CLI, dashboard, or docs when a capability needs them, with the owning team reviewing.

    Review code and designs, mentor other engineers, and grow into leading the team’s technical direction.

    Have 5+ years of experience as a software engineer, most of it building and running backend services in production.

    Have run a high-traffic, multi-tenant service in production: been on call for it, worked incidents through to resolution, and followed through on postmortems.

    Write strong TypeScript, and work confidently in a large Node.js backend codebase.

    Understand Postgres from the client side: connection management and pooling, transactions, statement timeouts and cancellation, and large result sets.

    Have built observability for a service you owned (metrics, tracing, logs, and alerts tied to SLOs), and used it to debug problems that span proxies, load balancers, or Kubernetes.

    Have kept a service healthy under load with patterns such as rate limiting, timeouts, memory limits, and graceful degradation.

    Have shipped changes to a live service safely, with canaries, staged rollouts, feature flags, or fast rollback.

    Work calmly and constructively with other teams during incidents, including when the root cause is in a system you don’t own.

    Communicate clearly in writing, from design docs to postmortems, thrive in async, globally distributed teams, and make progress when the path isn’t fully defined.

    Nice to have, roughly in order of how much they’d help:.

    Have rebuilt or migrated a live, high-traffic service without breaking its callers, using techniques such as shadow traffic, contract tests, or incremental replacement.

    Have led the design of reliability work, such as tenant isolation, load shedding, or a staged-deploy pipeline, or set technical direction that other engineers built on.

    Have built or operated a database proxy or connection pooler (such as PgBouncer, Supavisor, or pgcat), or an API gateway such as Envoy.

    Have secured a service that runs SQL on its callers’ behalf: handling credentials safely, and limiting how much damage any one caller can do.

    Production experience in a second backend language, such as Elixir or Go.

    Experience with a secrets manager or key management service, such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS KMS.

    Familiarity with Supabase, or with how AI agents use databases through tools like MCP.

    Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Sources indicate that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the tech giant. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are notable to us.

    It has been revealed that once a year, the entire company gathers in a fresh city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Sources indicate that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    Account Manager at Atticus

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government.
    • Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid.
    • So far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid. Our mission is to tear down barriers between people in crisis and the aid they deserve. In the last six years, we’ve become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We also help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    So far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews. And we’re just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, Google Ventures, and True Ventures, and we’re on our way to creating a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    According to recent reports, in the next two years, we aim to help over 250,000 Americans get access to life-changing benefits. Much of that help reaches people through our Lawyer Network: our network of vetted partner law firms that represent clients alongside Atticus. The Lawyer Network (LN) team, led by Erin Casale, is the bridge between Atticus and those firms, and our job is to improve their ability to serve clients and help them grow.

    We're hiring a Senior Account Manager to own our largest partner firms. You'll carry a deliberately small book of high-volume firms (roughly 10) and act as an extension of their team: diagnosing where and why they lose cases, coaching them on operations and legal execution, and getting even the most technophobic firm to adopt fresh Atticus tools.

    The ideal candidate has spent years making small business customers measurably better at what they do through a mix of operations and tech, and wants to do that work somewhere it changes lives.

    Make firms better. Own our enterprise-tier partner firms and improve their capacity, conversion rates, and win rates. Find best practices in firm operations and Social Security Disability legal execution, spread them across the network, and coach them relentlessly.

    Drive technology adoption. Get every firm, including folks who are tech-hesitant, using new Atticus features well. That means making the case for the value (think: sales motion but the product is free), building and implementing change management plans, and running training and support.

    Know your firms from the inside. Build relationships beyond the managing attorney, down to intake, case development, and operations leads. Understand a firm well enough to help with hiring, software, and staffing decisions, not just Atticus problems.

    According to recent reports, be the voice of firms inside Atticus. Bring what you learn back to Product, Customer Experience, and Operations so we serve firms better and learn from their experience.

    Deliver hard news well. Hold firms to clear performance standards and push back on attorneys—even those with decades of experience in the field—with finesse and confidence. If needed, cut ties gracefully.

    Shape how the team works. Own strategic projects end to end, from scoping the question and gathering data to sharing recommendations with leadership and rolling out what works across the network.

    5+ years in Account Management, Customer Success, Partnerships, or a similar role serving small businesses, where your mandate was improving your accounts' performance (not just retention).

    A track record of driving product adoption in a tech or tech-adjacent setting.

    You read data comfortably, spot trends before results move, and show up with both a diagnosis and a strategy.

    You're persuasive in conversation and in writing, and you'd rather pick up the phone (or get on a plane) than send another email.

    You're outgoing and build trust rapidly, with colleagues and with skeptical partners alike.

    Adaptable: resourceful and steady when priorities shift.

    You pick up upcoming tools fast, from cloud software to building a clean deck.

    According to recent reports, we covered above why this job might be for you, and think it’s equally vital to tell you why it might not be for you. You won’t enjoy this job very much if:.

    You prefer a large book of light-touch accounts over depth with a few.

    You want a predictable playbook.

    You get frustrated when projects and priorities change rapidly (we obviously try to limit this, but are a quickly-growing company and it does still happen).

    Recent findings suggest that the role is a rare opportunity to join a fast-growing Series C startup that doubles as a B-corp social enterprise. Our team is still small enough for you to have an outsized impact on how we operate and how our firms grow.

    We offer competitive pay, including equity, and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employee and family premiums covered.

    15 vacation days and ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at end-of-year).

    $1,000 reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    Sources indicate that we anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $110,000 and $130,000, in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as the candidate's experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    This job is fully remote and we're committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the manufacturer dime) as needed to be with your colleagues, usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather. You'll also visit partner firms in-person occasionally. Overall, expect to travel up to monthly between internal get togethers and firm visits.

    #169433. Breaking: The Kitchen Trends Designers Expect to See Everywhere in 2027

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (531 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: The Kitchen Trends Designers Expect to See Everywhere in 2027

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Above: the kitchen of an Athens home designed by Nashmita Rajiah.
    • Partial walls, hidden appliances, and pantries with room for prep are among the kitchen features expected to gain ground next year, according to the National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 Kitchen Trends Report.
    • NKBA reports growing interest in partial walls, movable partitions, and separate kitchen zones—a shift from last year’s forecast, when open layouts were still gaining ground.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Above: the kitchen of an Athens home designed by Nashmita Rajiah.

    Partial walls, hidden appliances, and pantries with room for prep are among the kitchen features expected to gain ground next year, according to the National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 Kitchen Trends Report. Based on a survey of 830 kitchen-industry professionals—including designers, manufacturers, remodelers, and architects—the report looks at the layouts, materials, lighting, and technology they expect to be popular over the next three years. Here are the main takeaways.

    NKBA reports growing interest in partial walls, movable partitions, and separate kitchen zones—a shift from last year’s forecast, when open layouts were still gaining ground. Dedicated prep spaces and back kitchens are also emerging features, cited by nearly half of designers.

    Kitchens are still expected to get bigger, with 52 percent of designers anticipating growth. The kitchen’s surrounding rooms are growing, too. NKBA reports that mudrooms and laundry spaces are increasingly being integrated into kitchen looks. The vast majority of designers expect attached mudrooms to be popular over the next three years, with 45 percent anticipating mudrooms getting larger and 43 percent expecting laundry spaces to grow.

    In a recent development, appliances are increasingly being incorporated into cabinetry rather than left on display. Eighty-five percent of designers agree cabinets are being designed to hide appliances and other functional elements, and roughly two-thirds say open shelving is on its way out in favor of enclosed storage.

    It has been revealed that pantries are taking on more work, too. Nearly 90 percent agree they are becoming multifunctional extensions of the kitchen, and three-quarters expect dedicated small-appliance stations to be popular. Separate beverage areas continue to gain support, with 90 percent anticipating their popularity, up from 85 percent in the 2026 report.

    Neutrals remain the leading color of choice, followed by greens and blues. For cabinetry, light and medium tones draw equal interest, and white oak is the preferred wood for roughly half of designers. Islands don’t necessarily have to match: a little more than half expect them to feature a different color from the surrounding cabinets. Quartzite and quartz lead countertop preferences, with nearly half of designers favoring honed or matte finishes.

    Industry observers note that the lighting forecast includes under-cabinet lights, illuminated cabinet interiors, nighttime path lighting, sconces, and pendants. Eighty-four percent of designers agree kitchens will incorporate multiple layers of light, and 78 percent say lighting is increasingly being used as a design feature rather than just a functional necessity. Under-cabinet lighting leads the forecast at 87 percent, followed by interior-cabinet lighting at 76 percent.

    In a recent development, NKBA identifies ventilation, water filtration, touchless faucets, and sound-absorbing materials among the report’s wellness features. Designers are also discussing ways to make kitchens more resilient: 65 percent cite leak-detection systems and automatic shut-off valves, 62 percent cite backup power, and a little over half point to ventilation and air filtration.

    Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more.

    Enterprise customers trust us with real-time audio, video and data belonging to their own end users, and before they build on LiveKit they want proof that we protect it. You will share the day-to-day running of the compliance program with the rest of our Compliance team. We want someone who works themselves out of a job on the repeatable work. You will automate and simplify what you own, so your time goes to the larger deals and our compliance work grows more slowly than our customer base. We run SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS and HIPAA today, with ISO 9001 in progress. This role is remote, based in the United States or Canada.

    I’ve tested many mattresses, and Saatva’s Classic Mattress remains my favorite. It balances plush cushioning with supportive lift, and in my experience, it feels even better than the mattresses I’ve slept on at luxury hotels. It’s worth the investment.

    It has been revealed that for a mattress designed to please every type of sleeper, opt for Saatva’s Classic style. It’s a sturdy mattress complete with a hybrid coils-meet-foam design. Available in three different firmness settings, you’ll get a plush, cloud-like feel from the cushioned foam top layer, which is set on top of pressure-relieving coils that contour to your body.

    It has been revealed that with my Luxury Firm mattress, I can feel myself sinking into the pillow top as soon as I lie down, while the supportive layers underneath help realign my body and take the pressure off my back and shoulders. I can comfortably sleep on my back or sides, and it has helped reduce body pains.

    Beyond the popular Classic mattress, Saatva has a range of specialized models that cater to specific sleep concerns or lifestyle preferences, including mattresses made from organic latex and cooling memory foam options.

    Perhaps Saatva’s most innovative model, the Rx mattress is specifically designed for those with chronic back or joint conditions like sciatica, arthritis, scoliosis, or a herniated disc. It has specialized lumbar zones for spinal alignment and extra support to alleviate pressure from the body.

    For those who prefer an eco-conscious or hypoallergenic bed, Saatva’s Latex Hybrid and Zenhaven models are made from organic latex that is naturally cooling. The Zenhaven is the brand’s more premium option with dual-sided firmness (meaning you can flip it over when you’re craving a change).

    The Memory Foam mattress is ideal for side sleepers, while the cooling qualities of the Contour5 make it a nice option for those who find memory foam hot. But if you’re sharing a bed with a partner who has different sleep preferences, opt for the Solaire, which has 50 firmness settings on each side, so no one has to compromise.

    Take the brand’s online mattress quiz to help you make your decision.

    Should you wind up unhappy with your Saatva mattress, the brand offers a 365-night home trial. If you’re not satisfied, you can return your mattress for a full refund or exchange it for another model within the trial period—just note that returns and exchanges are subject to a $99 pickup and processing fee.

    Industry observers note that your mattress purchase comes with free white-glove delivery, which includes in-home setup and removal of your old mattress—so all you need to do is select which luxe bedding you want to add to it. Plus, Saatva’s mattresses are backed by a lifetime warranty, which covers any defects or repairs.

    #169402. 5 Fall Trends Designers Think Will Still Look Good Next Spring

    📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (969 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

    5 Fall Trends Designers Think Will Still Look Good Next Spring

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Above: A hallway view of Eric Egan’s Milan apartment.
    • If any season has the power to inspire a complete aesthetic overhaul, it’s fall.
    • Recent findings suggest that this fall in particular, designers are urging clients to trust their guts—making sure they see themselves in the spaces they create, rather than blindly following the latest fads.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Above: A hallway view of Eric Egan’s Milan apartment.

    If any season has the power to inspire a complete aesthetic overhaul, it’s fall. Nature’s changing palette inspires us to follow suit, as each year our mood boards make new space for jewel tones, cozy textures, and a bottomless candle budget. Autumnal trends are so alluring, it almost feels like a risky time to make long-term design decisions. But with the right consideration, that seasonal inspiration can translate into choices that look good year-round.

    Recent findings suggest that this fall in particular, designers are urging clients to trust their guts—making sure they see themselves in the spaces they create, rather than blindly following the latest fads. “For me, a trend has to be authentic or it’s just noise,” claims designer Chad Dorsey, who’s eager to ditch the spare minimalism of years past for looks with more personality. ELLE Decor A-Lister Kerry Joyce seconds the motion: “By prioritizing personalized storytelling, a space becomes evergreen, evolving as smaller objects are swapped out over time.”.

    But an expert nudge in the right direction never hurts. This fall, top designers are gravitating toward creative color-drenching, cleverly concealed storage, tactile upholstery, and rooms built around art. Read on for their takes on the fall 2026 trends worth investing in, plus tips on building (as Dorsey puts it) “spaces designed to be lived in, not looked at.”.

    In a recent development, fabric and upholstery are trending ultra plush and textured for fall, but when thoughtfully integrated, they feel more timeless than seasonal. “Design is shifting toward how a space feels, not just how it looks,” states Joyce, who’s seeing an increased popularity in fabrics like mohair, velvet, cashmere, and alpaca hair. “This focus on texture does more than elevate a room's aesthetic,” he explains. “It creates a sensory experience that comforts the soul.”.

    Start your bedroom redesign this fall and your space will strike the perfect balance between fresh and lived-in by spring. Between client requests and a personal home build, Amber Lewis has bedrooms on the brain right now. One trend takes the lead in her eyes: “I love matching the walls to the bed upholstery and bedding so the whole room feels wrapped in one warm color family. It’s calm and peaceful, and that enveloping feeling works in any season.”.

    Luckily, this cozy trend doesn’t require a complete room overhaul: “The easiest place to start is the bed itself. Reupholster your headboard in a pattern you love, or drape a vintage suzani across the foot of the bed,” Lewis says. “One move like that changes the whole mood of the room without starting over.” To bring in a little dimension and pop, she recommends adding a singular statement, like a lone striped pillow.

    If your primary suite needs a more holistic update, Lewis recommends creating a small sitting area. Sourcing vintage chairs and small sofas for primary suites this fall has given Lewis a newly introduced perspective on where bedroom design is headed: “True sanctuaries that feel layered, personal, and built for actually living in.”.

    Color drenching isn’t going anywhere for fall 2026—or long after, according to Dorsey. When choosing a shade for a room, he finds that any color works harder when it’s layered and intentional. Color capping—a term coined by Benjamin Moore referring to painting a room in multiple tones from one color family—can help keep a space from feeling flat or overwhelmed beneath a statement hue.

    According to Dorsey, the staying power of color drenching goes hand in hand with the shift away from spareness and toward “collected” spaces: “Neither is really a ‘look;’ they’re about living with things you love, which is why they’ll carry well into spring.”.

    Recent findings suggest that designer Regan Baker notes that cleverly hidden space solutions are also on the rise. “It could be a TV that slides behind a commissioned art panel, a Murphy bed tucked into a wall of millwork or that serves as a desk when it's stored, or a peg wall that’s a place to hang a jacket one minute and a standing desk the next,” she says. These solutions are tailored to her clients’ spaces (rather than tied to a season or palette), which gives them staying power.

    According to recent reports, this concept is an easy way to turn the corner you’ve never known how to style into your favorite part of the room. “In an existing home, look at the awkward spots, like an alcove or the wall around a fireplace, and treat built-ins there as a design moment instead of an afterthought,” Baker advises.

    If there’s one built-to-last fall trend most designers can agree on, it’s added eccentricity. “Homes are steering away from the sterile, overnight look of a showroom delivery,” Joyce notes. “The defining philosophy now focuses on layering modern staples with antiques, secondhand finds, travel mementos, and new pieces that carry a sense of patina.”.

    Dorsey describes this style as “collected rather than prescribed,” where a high-low mix of vintage and custom elements gel together. And while it may feel loftier than a trending, sold-out piece, Baker claims that most clients start with an artistic anchor, then build around it: “We’re designing more homes around a piece of art than around a color trend. That might be wallpaper by local designers, a commissioned piece, or even a palette pulled from a lichen-covered rock found on the property.”.

    One key takeaway? Curate like a collector. Your reward may be a space that never goes out of style.

    Grace McCarty is a freelance Associate Digital Editor at ELLE Decor, where she covers design trends, shopping, and culture. She previously held a staff position at SELF Magazine, where she focused on beauty, style, and wellness. Her work has also appeared in Glamour and Parade.

    #169382. I Just Finished My Kitchen Renovation, and This “Hidden” Island Feature Is the One Upgrade I’d Recommend to Everyone

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (832 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    I Just Finished My Kitchen Renovation, and This “Hidden” Island Feature Is the One Upgrade I’d Recommend to Everyone

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, I’m always noticing something cool in someone else’s home and thinking, “Oh, I need that, too.” That happened last year when my family stayed with my in-laws.
    • It was simple, practical, and exactly the kind of feature I wanted in my own kitchen.
    • Ahead, here’s why I love having a pop-up outlet, what to consider before installing one, and a few other kitchen gadgets that you might want to consider adding to your next upgrade.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, I’m always noticing something cool in someone else’s home and thinking, “Oh, I need that, too.” That happened last year when my family stayed with my in-laws. It was my first time seeing their newly renovated kitchen, and after a quick tour, one small detail caught my eye: the pop-up outlet in the kitchen island.

    It was simple, practical, and exactly the kind of feature I wanted in my own kitchen. When we recently renovated our cook space, it went to the top of our wish list—and it has indeed been a game-changer with how we use the area.

    Ahead, here’s why I love having a pop-up outlet, what to consider before installing one, and a few other kitchen gadgets that you might want to consider adding to your next upgrade.

    In a recent development, like the name suggests, a pop-up outlet is basically an electrical outlet that hides inside your countertop until you need it. Most models have a top you press or pull, and the outlet rises up so you can plug in your blender, mixer, or whatever else you're using. When you're done, you push it back down and it's out of sight.

    There are a few different versions, including ones that pop up manually and others that rise with the push of a button. Some, like the one we have, include USB ports or wireless charging built in. The outlet connects to power underneath the countertop, so it's something you'll want to plan for before your newly introduced counters go in.

    It has been revealed that like pretty much any kitchen gadget, there are a range of options available from budget to high end. We opted for something mid-tier that still included the main functions we wanted like the additional USB ports and the charging capability on the top. If you’re a chronic “let your phone get down to one or two percent before finally charging it” person like me, I highly recommend this.

    There also are some that will go nearly fully flush with the countertop, and can even have part of the countertop material on the top of it to look seamless. We did not go this route, but if you prefer the look of a flawless countertop, this might be the way to go.

    We put ours in the corner of our kitchen where it’s almost entirely hidden by decor. That corner of the kitchen was otherwise without any spots to plug in appliances, so this fixed multiple problems by having electricity access while remaining discreet.

    Sources indicate that you can really put them anywhere you want, but keep in mind where you’ll need extra power accessibility and where it won’t be an eyesore, if that’s a concern. I’m also a massive fan of in-drawer charging outlets.

    It has been revealed that there was some back-and-forth about adding this pop-up outlet to our kitchen remodel budget. The outlet itself isn’t break-the-bank expensive, but there were extra expenses that went with it, like hiring an electrician and paying to have a hole cut in the newly introduced countertop.

    Though we decided it was worth the expense, here are some of the pros and cons you should consider if you’re on the fence.

    I’m always so impressed by kitchens that integrate small, helpful gadgets like this one into their design. Here are a few other popular additions that we either made or were thinking about adding to our renovation.

    Maybe it’s just a me thing, but I feel like the harder it is to find an appliance or trash can, the fancier a kitchen is. The pull-out trash can was integrated into our kitchen peninsula, and we purchased a more expensive panel-ready dishwasher so it looked like a regular cabinet. An integrated refrigerator was almost twice as expensive as a regular one, so we did not go that route.

    With the way our kitchen is laid out, we unfortunately have two awkward corner cabinets. For one, we upgraded with blind corner cabinet hardware, which was well worth it.

    According to recent reports, we did not integrate a bottle rinser into our current kitchen design, but we did in our last two kitchens and loved them. It got so much use when our two kids were babies, since we could quickly rinse out bottles. They’re also great for wine drinkers or anyone who hosts a lot of parties.

    Industry observers note that admittedly, this one is controversial, as some designers don’t like this feature. But personally, we love the look and it’s next on our “cool kitchen wish list.”.

    Follow House Beautiful on Instagram and TikTok.

He has written for multiple home improvement magazines and websites, drawing on his own experience renovating homes with his wife to create practical, inspiring content for homeowners and DIY enthusiasts alike.

    #169379. Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

    📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1839 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011.
    • Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.
    • Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call).

    Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

    Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

    In a recent development, A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous Fresh York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

    According to recent reports, sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

    In a recent development, “Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito stated. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”.

    According to recent reports, west Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

    “His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

    Recent findings suggest that rockefeller was born in Latest York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

    It has been revealed that he returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

    Sources indicate that in West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness.".

    According to recent reports, he had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

    It has been revealed that rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

    Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

    Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

    Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

    According to recent reports, but defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

    But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

    Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

    He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”.

    Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

    In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him mentioned the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

    In a recent development, he believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

    In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

    He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

    Recent findings suggest that but industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

    “The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he remarked on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”.

    His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

    It has been revealed that he had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller confirmed he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

    Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

    In a recent development, rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance proposal, he remarked, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”.

    According to recent reports, "These are people," Rockefeller said, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice.".

    The amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

    Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

    Recent findings suggest that rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

    According to recent reports, respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

    Recent findings suggest that rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

    Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (479 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: 5 Ways Warmth Has Shaped Interior Design in 2026, According to Experts

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (479 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After years of cool neutrals and minimalist interiors, there’s been a shift toward warmer, more inviting spaces that feel layered, personal, and lived-in.
    • “Warmth has become more than just a color palette or a particular material.
    • It has been revealed that at the end of the day, a warm home should feel inviting and effortless, with materials and details that make people want to spend time there.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After years of cool neutrals and minimalist interiors, there’s been a shift toward warmer, more inviting spaces that feel layered, personal, and lived-in.

    “Warmth has become more than just a color palette or a particular material. It's about spaces that feel authentic, comfortable, and reflective of the people who live in them,” says Laura Gerber, an interior designer, project manager, and production coordinator with ODE Design.

    It has been revealed that at the end of the day, a warm home should feel inviting and effortless, with materials and details that make people want to spend time there. If you’re looking to add some warmth to your home, take inspiration from these designer-approved ideas.

    Wood’s organic grain brings instant warmth to both modern and traditional homes, adding depth without making a space feel overly formal.

    “We’re incorporating more white oak, walnut, and rift-cut cabinetry than we have in years, along with wood ceilings and paneled walls,” explains Rachel Simpson, senior interior designer at Revive Design and Renovation.

    Sources indicate that there’s been a shift from stark white countertops toward natural quartzite, travertine, and marble with warmer veining. These materials have natural variation and movement that bring character into a space.

    It has been revealed that “Honed finishes, in particular, feel softer and more organic than high-polish surfaces. They allow the beauty of the stone to speak for itself without feeling overly formal or glossy,” explains Simpson.

    These days, people really want their homes to feel like a sanctuary.

    According to recent reports, “In a recent project, the client envisioned a grown-up treehouse nestled among the evergreens. We wanted to create a warm yet contemporary mountain retreat that felt luxurious but also comfortable and welcoming,” notes Charles Greenfeld, founder and principal designer at Ethan Charles Design.

    Rather than relying on one or two dramatic statement pieces, the interiors were designed to be experienced as a whole, with each detail contributing to that warm aesthetic.

    Industry observers note that creating warmth is really about creating layers of thoughtfully curated design elements. This helps to create a home you want to enter and never leave.

    “Well-proportioned rugs, textures on walls, loads of art, draperies, and lighting overhead and at eye level are just some of the things we can add to our spaces to make them feel cozy and accessible,” says Ashley Powell, cofounder and interior designer of Roseberry Allen.

    Designers have lately been drawn to rooms where the colors are close to one another, but the materials do different things.

    “A woven rug, a textured wall, and a piece of wood with a visible grain each catch the light differently,” says Jess Klein, founder and principal of Jess Klein Studio.

    That variation adds visual depth and makes the room feel warmer and more inviting, even when the color palette is understated.

    OpenAI Getting Rid of Custom GPTs and Moving to Plugin Architecture

    📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OpenAI has announced it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a fresh plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.
    • Custom GPT retirement is presently scheduled for Dec.
    • For affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OpenAI has announced it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a fresh plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.

    Custom GPT retirement is presently scheduled for Dec. 11, 2026, although the manufacturer says timing and migration availability can vary by account and workspace.

    For affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct. 26 for ending creation of latest Custom GPTs. Qualifying Enterprise customers with approved deferrals can continue using them until Feb. 11, 2027.

    OpenAI has changed its UI to make GPTs less prominent, and when users choose to try creating a newly introduced Custom GPT, they are now prompted with an option to create a plugin instead.

    Rather than maintaining separate customized versions of ChatGPT, OpenAI is shifting customization toward plugins that can package reusable instructions, reference material, and connections to outside services.

    Under OpenAI's plugin architecture, a plugin can include one or more skills containing instructions and resources for repeatable workflows, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing tools and external systems, or both. ChatGPT and Codex share a universal plugin directory, although some capabilities can remain specific to a particular environment.

    For organizations, that makes the change more than a simple renaming exercise. A firm could package recurring workflows into skills while using MCP servers or connected apps to give those workflows access to enterprise systems and data.

    In a recent development, openAI claims creators will be able to migrate an existing GPT through the My GPTs interface. The GPT's instructions become a skill in the replacement plugin, while knowledge files are copied into plugin reference files and connected apps can be carried over.

    Recent findings suggest that not everything transfers automatically. Existing GPT conversations do not migrate, the selected model does not carry over, and Custom Actions may have to be rebuilt using an available app or a custom MCP server.

    It has been revealed that sharing also changes. Migrated plugins start private, existing GPT owners do not automatically receive access to the replacement, and prior sharing settings do not carry over.

    Sources indicate that openAI is also cautioning organizations against assuming that migration will preserve behavior exactly. "A migrated plugin may respond differently," the company says, recommending that consumers retest familiar prompts, reference-material use, required output formats, and integrations before relying on the replacement.

    It has been revealed that that warning has contributed to pushback from some GPT builders, who argue that plugins do not fully reproduce the dedicated and predictable environment of a Custom GPT. Other complaints have focused on sharing, migration complexity, and differences in how migrated workflows use instructions and reference material.

    Sources indicate that despite those concerns, OpenAI is clearly consolidating around plugins as its common mechanism for extending its AI products. Its developer documentation now describes plugins as packages owners can "discover, install, share, and publish" across ChatGPT and Codex, replacing the separate-custom-assistant model with reusable AI capabilities that can be combined with enterprise tools and services.

    For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

    David Ramel is an editor and writer at Converge 360.

    📅 05 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (810 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    AI Ambitions Are Running Into a Network Infrastructure Trust Problem

    📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.
    • The research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years.
    • The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.

    The research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years. Among respondents whose initiatives were affected, AI and data-driven projects were the most cited, at 49%. That put AI ahead of security and compliance programs at 44%, digital transformation at 42%, and cloud migration at 38%.

    The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.

    Sources indicate that all respondents worked for organizations with more than 2,000 employees and influenced network strategy across data centers, cloud, and connectivity. Of those surveyed, 66% had final sign-off responsibility. The results suggest that as organizations pursue increasingly data-intensive AI projects, confidence in the network infrastructure supporting them could become another deployment obstacle.

    According to recent reports, on the surface, Arelion found little evidence of a trust crisis. A total of 93% of respondents stated they largely or completely trust their current network provider, while 83% said that trust has strengthened over time.

    The picture changes when respondents are asked about a serious network incident. Only 15% said they have complete confidence in their provider's ability to promptly detect and address such a problem. Another 42% said their provider seriously lets them down anywhere from a few times a year to monthly or more frequently.

    In a recent development, those concerns have consequences beyond the network itself. Responding organizations have delayed, scaled back, or stopped strategic initiatives because of provider trust concerns, while others have added resiliency or risk-mitigation measures.

    AI and data projects were the most affected among respondents reporting an impact, as organizations try to move AI from experimentation into larger production deployments.

    A serious provider failure could also have substantial consequences. Forty percent of respondents said such an event would cause major operational disruption, while 18% anticipated significant financial loss or severe financial or reputational damage.

    Industry observers note that another tension runs through Arelion's findings. Enterprises need networks they can trust to support AI projects, but many of the same decision-makers are concerned about AI's growing role inside those networks. A total of 54% of respondents identified AI and automation in network management and security as the factors most likely to negatively affect network trust over the next three years. That ranked ahead of data sovereignty expectations and geopolitical instability, both at 39%, and regulatory requirements and quantum computing threats to current encryption standards, both at 38%.

    At the same time, respondents aren't rejecting AI as a network technology. Proactive AI-driven fault prediction was among the capabilities they stated would matter most to future trust, alongside stronger built-in security, greater accountability, and responsive support. That leaves enterprises in an unusual position: AI is increasing their dependence on digital infrastructure while also raising questions about how that infrastructure itself is managed.

    In a recent development, arelion has an interest in emphasizing the importance of network-provider trust, and the survey reflects the views specifically of network decision-makers at large enterprises. Still, the findings point to an infrastructure consideration that can get lost amid the rush to adopt new AI models and agents. AI projects ultimately depend on the networks, cloud environments, data centers, and connectivity beneath them. If organizations lack confidence in that foundation, access to better AI models alone won't remove the obstacle.

    Industry observers note that "Trust is influencing which strategic initiatives move forward, how organizations manage risk, and which providers they choose to work with," noted Mattias Fridström, Vice President at Arelion. "As businesses become increasingly reliant on digital infrastructure, enterprises are looking for network providers that can demonstrate transparency, accountability, and operational excellence, not just availability.".

    The full report is available for download here at the Arelion site (registration required).
